HIPAA, Confidentiality & Ethical Writing

Workplace product

Confidentiality incident / case response

Course goals advanced

  • 4. Documentation-Style Writing and Professional Responsibility
  • 2. Professional Workplace Writing
  • 3. Patient-Centered Communication

Spiraling back

This topic revisits grammar you met earlier, in a harder context: Topic 3, Topic 7.

1

Essential Question

What should I communicate, to whom, and how much information is appropriate?

2

Teaching & Learning Concepts

The communication principles, workplace expectations, and healthcare context behind this topic.

  • The minimum necessary principle — disclose what the purpose requires and no more
  • Confidentiality in writing, including in messages you consider informal
  • Appropriate audience: who actually needs to know this?
  • Professional boundaries in written communication
  • Public versus private communication, and how easily the line moves
  • Digital communication risks — forwarding, screenshots, and shared screens
3

Grammar Focus

A small set of high-value grammar skills, tied directly to this topic's communication task.

Clarity and precision

  • Vague pronouns that leave the reader guessing who is meant
  • Ambiguous wording that could describe two different situations
  • Pronoun–noun agreement
  • Revising unclear sentences until only one reading is possible

5

Formative Practice

Guided activities and short exercises. None of this is graded — it is here so you can find out what you know before it counts.

Who needs to know?

For each disclosure, decide whether it meets the minimum necessary standard.

Practice only — nothing here is graded or recorded.

  • Sending records for one date of service to a specialist who requested them for that visit.

    Sort this statement

  • Sending the complete chart because it is quicker than pulling the relevant pages.

    Sort this statement

  • Telling a colleague on the care team the patient's diagnosis so they can prepare the room appropriately.

    Sort this statement

  • Mentioning in the break room that a patient you both know came in today.

    Sort this statement

  • Answering a spouse's phone question about the visit, with no authorization on file.

    Sort this statement

  • Including the diagnosis code on a claim submitted to the patient's insurer.

    Sort this statement
Sort all 6 first.

Rewrite the unsafe message

Each of these was sent. Rewrite so it does the job without the exposure.

Self-scored practice. Your writing stays in this browser.

  • 1

    As written

    Team — heads up that Maria Alvarez from the front desk's sister is coming in this afternoon for the thing we talked about. Be discreet!

    The problem: Names the patient, identifies her by her relationship to a staff member, hints at the condition, and broadcasts it to a group. 'Be discreet' does not undo any of that.

    Write your version first — comparing before you try teaches nothing.

  • 2

    As written

    She said she'd been having those symptoms since the thing last year and she thinks it might be related to it.

    The problem: Every noun has been replaced by a pronoun or 'thing'. A reader cannot tell what symptoms, what event, or what she thinks is related.

    Write your version first — comparing before you try teaches nothing.

6

Cumulative Workplace Product

Combine this topic's grammar, vocabulary, and communication skills into something you would actually produce at work.

Confidentiality incident / case response

Analyze a confidentiality scenario and produce an appropriate written response: what happened, who needed to know, what should have been disclosed instead, and what you would do now.

Submit through Brightspace. This page is for drafting and self-checking.

7

Revision & Reflection

Review your work against the Communication Check, then name one thing to improve next time.

Communication Check

Check your own writing against all five. Not graded — saved in this browser only.

Communication Check — check each criterion your writing meets

Think about

  • For each disclosure in your response, name the purpose it served.
  • Would the patient be comfortable reading what you wrote about them?
  • Is there anything here that identifies the patient indirectly?
